pages.summary: The sum of the elements, down the columns by default.
body: Of a vector, the sum of its elements; of a matrix, a row of column sums. Give a dimension to sum along another way (2 for the rows), or `'all'` for one total. A `NaN` makes the sum `NaN` unless `'omitnan'` leaves it out.
syntax: The sums down the first dimension whose length is not 1.

examples.title: A vector, the columns and the rows of a matrix
examples.code:
sum([1 2 3 4])
A = [1 2 3; 4 5 6];
colSums = sum(A)
rowSums = sum(A, 2)
total = sum(A, 'all')

examples.title: Counting with logical values
examples.intro: A comparison gives true (1) or false (0), so its sum counts the elements that pass.

pages.summary: The product of the elements, down the columns by default.
body: Of a vector, the product of its elements; of a matrix, a row of the column products. `prod(1:n)` is n factorial.
syntax: The products down the first dimension whose length is not 1.

examples.title: A factorial, and the products of columns and rows

pages.summary: Cumulative sums.
body: Each element of the result is the sum of the elements up to and including that point, down the columns by default. The last element of `cumsum(v)` is `sum(v)`.
syntax: Running sums down the first dimension whose length is not 1.
Running sums from the end back to the start.

examples.title: A random walk
examples.code:
rng default
steps = sign(randn(1, 200));
plot(cumsum(steps))
xlabel('step')
ylabel('position')

pages.summary: The average.
body: The sum of the elements divided by their number, down the columns by default. A `NaN` makes the mean `NaN` unless `'omitnan'` leaves it out; `'Weights'` gives a weighted average.
syntax: The averages down the first dimension whose length is not 1.

examples.title: Of a vector, and of the columns and rows of a matrix

pages.summary: The middle value.
body: The value in the middle when the elements are sorted, or the average of the two middle ones when their number is even; down the columns by default. Unlike the mean, it is not pulled far by a few extreme values.
syntax: The medians down the first dimension whose length is not 1.

examples.title: Odd and even numbers of values

pages.summary: The standard deviation and the variance.
body: The variance is the average squared distance from the mean, normalized by N-1 (the unbiased estimate from a sample) unless `w` is 1, which normalizes by N. The standard deviation is its square root, in the units of the data. Both go down the columns by default.
syntax: The standard deviation, normalized by N-1.
With `w` 0 (N-1) or 1 (N), or a vector of weights.
With a normalization or weights, along dimension `dim`.
With `NaN` values left out (and the same for `var`).

examples.title: A sample's spread
examples.code:
x = [4 8 6 5 3 7];
s = std(x)
v = var(x)
s^2 - v

examples.title: Along the rows of a matrix

pages.summary: The largest or smallest elements, or the larger or smaller of two arrays element by element.
body: Of a vector, its largest (or smallest) element, and with a second output its position; of a matrix, a row of column maxima. With two arrays, the larger (smaller) of each pair of elements. `NaN` is left out unless every element is `NaN`.
syntax: The largest elements down the first dimension whose length is not 1.
With the index of the first largest element.
The larger of each pair of elements (a scalar `B` caps from below).
The smallest elements, and the same forms as `max`.

examples.title: The largest value and where it is
Columns, rows and the whole matrix

pages.summary: Sort the elements, down the columns by default.
body: Numbers sort in increasing order (`'descend'` for decreasing); `NaN` goes to the end. A second output gives the indices that put the elements in order, so other arrays can be sorted to match. Text sorts too: a cell array of character vectors or a string array.
syntax: Each column (or a vector) in increasing order.
With the indices: `B` is `A(I)` for a vector.

examples.title: Sorting one array by another

pages.summary: The distinct values, sorted (or in the order first met).
body: Each value appears once in the result. Extra outputs map between the two: `C = A(ia)` and `A = C(ic)`, so `ic` labels each element with its group, ready for counting with `accumarray`. Works for numbers, text in cell or string arrays, and rows with `'rows'`.
syntax: In the order they first appear.
The distinct rows of a matrix.

examples.title: Distinct values, sorted and as first met
Counting each value

pages.summary: Differences between neighbours, or the nth differences.
body: `diff(x)` is `[x(2)-x(1), x(3)-x(2), …]`, one element shorter than `x`. Divided by the spacing it approximates a derivative; `diff(x, 2)` takes differences twice. For a matrix it works down the columns.

examples.title: A derivative by differences

pages.summary: Counts of values in bins.
body: Sorts the values into bins and counts each bin: the numbers a histogram draws, without drawing it. The bins are chosen from the data unless their number or their edges are given. A value equal to an inner edge falls in the bin to its right; the last bin includes its right edge.
syntax: Counts in bins chosen from the data, and the bins' edges.
In bins with the given edges.
With the bin each value fell in.

examples.title: Which bin each value fell in

pages.summary: Whether any element, or every element, is nonzero.
body: Down the columns by default, like `sum`; give a dimension or `'all'` for another way. `any` of an empty array is false and `all` of an empty array is true. They are the usual way to turn an array of comparisons into one condition for `if`.
syntax: True for each column with at least one nonzero element.
True when any element at all is nonzero.
True for each column whose elements are all nonzero (and the same forms as `any`).

examples.title: Some, every and none
examples.output:
ans =

  logical

   1

ans =

  logical

   0

ans =

  logical

   0

examples.title: Columns and rows of a matrix
examples.output:
ans =

  1×3 logical array

   1   0   0

ans =

  2×1 logical array

   1
   1

examples.title: One condition for an if

pages.summary: The indices of the nonzero elements.
body: Usually given a comparison: `find(x > 3)` gives the positions where it holds. The indices count down the columns (linear indices); with two outputs, rows and columns. `find(X, n)` stops after the first `n`.
syntax: The linear indices of the nonzero elements.

examples.title: Rows and columns in a matrix

pages.summary: True when the arrays have the same size and values (NaN is never equal).
body: Compares whole arrays, not element by element: the sizes must agree and every value too. Numbers of different classes compare by value (`isequal(1, int8(1))` is true). Text, cells and structs compare their contents. `NaN` is not equal to itself; `isequaln` treats two `NaN`s as equal.
syntax: True when every argument equals the first.

examples.title: Text and structs

pages.summary: Cumulative products.
body: Each element of the result is the product of the elements up to and including that point, down the columns by default. Growth factors compound this way: `cumprod(1 + r)` turns a series of returns into the growth of one unit.
syntax: Running products down the first dimension whose length is not 1.

pages.summary: The largest or smallest element so far.
body: Each element of the result is the largest (or smallest) of the elements up to that point: the running record, or the high-water mark of a series.
syntax: The running minimum (and the same forms).

examples.title: Records so far, and the fall from the peak
examples.code:
x = [3 5 2 8 6 9 4];
cummax(x)
cummin(x)
drawdown = cummax(x) - x

pages.summary: The most frequent value (the smallest of those tied).
body: Down the columns by default. With more outputs, how often it occurs and, as a cell array, every value tied for the most frequent.
syntax: The most frequent value of each column (or of a vector).
With every value tied for most frequent.

examples.title: The most frequent value, and ties

pages.summary: The smallest and largest elements.
body: The same as `min` and `max` together, in one pass.
syntax: The smallest and largest elements of each column (or of a vector).

examples.title: Of a vector and of a matrix's columns

pages.summary: The difference between the largest and smallest elements.
body: `max(A) - min(A)`, down the columns by default: the simplest measure of spread.
syntax: For each column (or of a vector).

pages.summary: Sort the rows of a matrix by its columns, or of a table by its variables.
body: Rows are ordered by their first column, ties broken by the second, and so on, keeping each row together. Columns can be chosen and ordered (negative for descending). With a second output, the order, to sort other data to match.
syntax: By the first column, then the next for ties.
By the columns listed, in that order.

examples.title: By one column, then by two

pages.summary: True when the elements are in sorted order.
body: Whether a vector is in increasing order (equal neighbours allowed). A quick check before an algorithm that needs sorted data, such as a binary search.
syntax: True when `A` is sorted in increasing order.

examples.title: Sorted and not
examples.output:
ans =

  logical

   1

ans =

  logical

   0

ans =

  logical

   1

pages.summary: Which elements of A are found in B, and where.
body: For each element of `A`, true when it occurs in `B`; the second output gives its position in `B` (0 when it does not occur). Works for numbers, text in cell or string arrays, and whole rows with `'rows'`.
syntax: True where the element of `A` is in `B`.
With the index in `B` of each one found.
For the rows of `A` among the rows of `B`.

pages.summary: Set operations: the values in either set, in both, in the first only, or in exactly one.
body: Each result holds every value once, sorted. The extra outputs say where the values came from: `C = A(ia)` and, for `union` and `intersect`, `C = B(ib)` for the values from `B`.
syntax: The values of `A` that are not in `B`.
The values in one but not both.
With where they are in `A` and `B` (and so for `union`; `setdiff` gives `ia`).

examples.title: The four operations

pages.summary: Counts of pairs in a grid of bins.
body: The bivariate histogram: each pair (x(k), y(k)) is counted in the bin of the grid it falls in. The bins are chosen from the data unless their numbers or edges are given.
syntax: Counts in a grid of bins chosen from the data.
With `nbins` bins in each direction (or `[nx ny]`).
With the edges and each pair's bin.

examples.title: The counts of correlated data, as an image

pages.summary: Counts of values between edges (the last bin holds values equal to the last edge).
body: An older form of counting: bin k counts the values with `edges(k) <= x < edges(k+1)`, and one more bin at the end counts the values equal to the last edge. `histcounts` is the newer form, whose last bin includes its right edge.
syntax: The counts, one for each edge.
With the bin of each value (0 outside the edges).

pages.summary: The bin each value falls into.
body: Gives each value the number of its bin among the edges (`NaN` outside them): a value equal to an inner edge goes to the bin to its right, and the last bin includes its right edge. With `n`, the bins are `n` equal ones over the data's range.
syntax: In `n` equal bins over the range of `X`.

pages.summary: The covariance of two vectors, or of the columns of a matrix.
body: For a matrix, each column is a variable and each row an observation: element (i, j) is the covariance of columns i and j, and the diagonal holds the variances. Normalized by N - 1 unless `w` is 1. `'omitrows'` leaves out rows with `NaN`.
syntax: The covariance matrix of the columns of `A`.
The 2-by-2 covariance matrix of two vectors.
With `w` 0 (N - 1) or 1 (N), or weights for the rows.

examples.title: The columns of a matrix, and the variances on the diagonal

pages.summary: Correlation coefficients.
body: The covariances scaled by the standard deviations: between -1 and 1, with 1 on the diagonal. A second output gives the p-values for the hypothesis of no correlation.
syntax: The correlation matrix of the columns of `A`.

examples.title: Correlated and uncorrelated columns

pages.summary: The running integral by the trapezoidal rule.
body: Like `trapz`, but every partial integral from the start: element k is the integral up to the k-th point. Velocity samples give the distance covered so far, rates give amounts.

examples.title: The integral of cos is sin

pages.summary: Quantiles and percentiles of a sample.
body: The value below which a given share of the data lies: `quantile(X, 0.5)` is the median and `prctile(X, 25)` the lower quartile. Between the data points, values are interpolated linearly. For a matrix, down the columns.
syntax: The quantiles for the probabilities `p` (between 0 and 1).

examples.title: The middle 90 percent of a sample

pages.summary: The interquartile range.
body: The difference between the third and first quartiles: the spread of the middle half of the data, little moved by outliers. Of a distribution object, the same for the distribution.
syntax: For each column (or of a vector).

pages.summary: The sample skewness and kurtosis.
body: The skewness measures asymmetry: 0 for symmetric data, positive when the right tail is longer. The kurtosis measures how heavy the tails are: 3 for the normal distribution (not the excess over 3). With `flag` 0 the bias of a small sample is corrected; 1 (the default) gives the plain sample values.
syntax: The skewness of each column (or of a vector).

examples.title: A symmetric sample and a skewed one

pages.summary: Statistics over a moving window.
body: Each element of the result is the statistic of a window of `k` neighbouring elements around it (for an even `k`, one more before than after), or of `kb` before and `kf` after. Near the ends the window shrinks to the elements there are. Moving means smooth noisy data; a moving median does so without being pulled by outliers.
syntax: The mean of each window of `k` elements.
The sum (and the same forms for `movprod`, `movmax`, `movmin`, `movmedian`, `movmad`, `movstd` and `movvar`).

examples.title: Smoothing noise, and an outlier

pages.summary: Scale values linearly to fill [0, 1], or another interval.
body: The smallest value goes to the lower end and the largest to the upper end, the others in proportion. `'InputMin'` and `'InputMax'` set the range taken as the input's, clamping what lies outside.

pages.summary: Centre and scale data (z-scores by default).
body: By default each column has its mean subtracted and is divided by its standard deviation, so that the result has mean 0 and standard deviation 1. Other methods scale to a norm, to a range, or by the median and interquartile range; the extra outputs give the centre and scale used, to apply the same to other data.
syntax: Z-scores of each column (or of a vector).
Centred on the median, scaled by the interquartile range.

examples.title: Z-scores, and their mean and spread

pages.summary: Where the local maxima (or minima) of data are.
body: A local maximum is higher than its neighbours on both sides; the first and last points never are. The prominence (the second output) says how far each stands out: the height above the higher of the lowest points between it and a higher peak on either side. `'MinProminence'` keeps the clear peaks only, and `'MinSeparation'` keeps peaks apart.
syntax: True at the local minima (and the same forms).

examples.title: Only the clear peaks

pages.summary: Where abrupt changes in data begin.
body: Splits the data into segments in which the mean (by default), the variance, or the slope and intercept of a line stay the same, and marks the first point of each new segment. `'Threshold'` sets how large a change must be (a cost for each change), and `'MaxNumChanges'` asks for the best split with at most that many.
syntax: [TF, S1, S2] = ischange(A, method, dim, 'Threshold', t, 'MaxNumChanges', k)
With conditions, and each segment's mean and variance (or slope and intercept).

examples.title: Steps in a level
Each segment's mean

pages.summary: Trends of data: long-term, seasonal and the remainder.
body: Splits a series into a long-term trend `LT`, seasonal trends `ST` (a column for each) and a remainder `R`, with `LT + sum(ST, 2) + R` equal to the data. By singular spectrum analysis (the default), or by STL with the period given.
syntax: With a lag of your own.
By STL, with the period (or periods) of the seasons.

examples.title: A rising series with a yearly cycle

pages.summary: The k smallest or largest elements.
body: The `k` smallest (largest) elements, smallest (largest) first, down the columns by default, with `NaN` last. The second output gives where they were.
syntax: By absolute value, with the indices.
The `k` largest elements (and the same forms).

examples.title: The three largest and smallest, and where they are

pages.summary: Values held between a lower and an upper bound.
body: Values below the lower bound become the lower bound, values above the upper bound the upper bound; `NaN` stays `NaN`.

pages.summary: Whether every element is finite, and whether any is NaN.
body: Quick checks of a whole array, giving one logical value: the same as `all(isfinite(A), 'all')` and `any(isnan(A), 'all')`.
syntax: True when no element is `Inf`, `-Inf` or `NaN`.

examples.title: Two arrays checked
examples.output:
ans =

  logical

   1

ans =

  logical

   0

ans =

  logical

   1

pages.summary: Whether a vector's values are evenly spaced.
body: True when the steps between neighbours are all the same, to round-off; the second output is the step (`NaN` when they are not).

pages.summary: An array padded or cut to a size.
body: `resize` makes an array the given length (or size), padding with a fill value (0 by default) or cutting as needed; `paddata` only pads and `trimdata` only cuts. Padding and cutting happen at the end unless `'Side'` says `'leading'` or `'both'`; `'Pattern'` pads by repeating the edge, the array, or its reflection.
syntax: `A` padded or cut to length `m` (or to the size `m`).
B = resize(A, m, 'Dimension', dim, 'Pattern', p, 'FillValue', v, 'Side', s)
Padded only, with the same options.

pages.summary: Distinct values and members of a set, values within a tolerance taken as one.
body: Floating-point results that should be equal often differ in their last digits; these compare with a tolerance relative to the largest value instead of exactly. `uniquetol` keeps one value of each group (its smallest), and `ismembertol` tests membership.
syntax: The distinct values, within 1e-6 relative to the largest.
True where a value of `A` is within the tolerance (1e-12 relative) of one of `B`.
With a tolerance, and where they are in `B`.

examples.title: Values that differ in their last digits

pages.summary: The root-mean-square error and the mean absolute percentage error.
body: Measures of how far a forecast or a model `F` is from the actual values `A`: `rmse` is `sqrt(mean(abs(F - A).^2))`, in the units of the data, and `mape` is `100*mean(abs((A - F)./A))`, in percent. Down the columns by default.
syntax: The mean absolute percentage error (and the same forms).

examples.title: A forecast against the actual values
